description: The control protocol between a service and a cluster coordinator: how a service registers, waits for its dependencies, becomes ready, and stays known.

A producer of this contract is a coordinator. Every other process in a cluster is a consumer of it, whatever else it also produces. The coordinator owns the registry, the selection policy and the handlers; this file owns the wire.
Registered and ready are distinct

Registered means the coordinator knows your coordinates. Ready means you are serving and your own consumed contracts have resolved. Only ready producers are ever handed out, so readiness is transitive and a cluster converges leaf-first, with no separate notion of whether the cluster as a whole is up.
The joining sequence

The ops below are listed in lifecycle order, and the order is part of the contract. A joiner calls `coord.register` with its instance id, its process id and every service it mounts; opens `coord.await_ready` and reads it to completion, receiving one binding per required consumed contract; calls `coord.ready`; and then calls `coord.heartbeat` on a repeating interval well under the coordinator's time-to-live for the rest of its life.

On a `unknown_instance` answer from either `coord.ready` or `coord.heartbeat`, the joiner re-registers and re-sends `coord.ready`. It must not re-run `coord.await_ready`: that is a one-shot startup step, its bindings are already in hand, and re-running it parks the process on dependencies it has already resolved.
Staying reachable is part of staying registered

Registration states where a process can be reached, and a process may go on running after some of that stops being true. A host that binds several transports keeps serving as long as any one of them is listening, so an accept loop that dies costs that transport and not the process — and the coordinates registered at startup then name an address that can only fail to dial. `coord.update` is how a joiner corrects that: whenever the set of transports it is actually answering on changes, it sends the coordinates it is serving on now, and the coordinator replaces what it holds.

The update carries the whole set rather than the part that changed. The sender is the only party that knows where it is listening, which makes a full replacement idempotent — sent twice, or sent after a reconnect that already re-registered the same coordinates, it changes nothing — where a delta would require the coordinator to hold a merge rule that the sender also holds. It follows that a registered service the update does not mention is left with no coordinates at all: a sender that under-reports makes a service unselectable, which is visible in a listing's unreachable field and is the conservative direction, whereas a merge would keep handing out the stale address that this op exists to withdraw.
A joiner that never loses a transport never sends this op, and a coordinator that never receives one behaves exactly as it always has.
Joining is a lifecycle, not a vocabulary

This file describes the ops, their shapes and their error codes exhaustively, and that is less than everything a joiner must do. It does not and cannot express: that the sequence above has that order; that a supervised child must write its probe file to the path in `PEERLINE_MANIFEST_OUT` and hold its lifeline descriptor open until end-of-file; that the coordinator's socket arrives in `PEERLINE_COORD_SOCK`; or that the host token in `Endpoints` must be derived exactly as `peerline.contract/1` says. An implementor needs the README beside this file as well as this file.
Why some failures are values and others are errors

Both appear, and the split is deliberate. A recoverable protocol state with one defined next step is a value: `unknown_instance` on ready or heartbeat means go and re-register, and a caller should not have to match an error code to drive its own state machine. A condition the caller cannot make progress against by retrying is an error: two processes claiming one identity, a second producer of a singleton contract, and a resolve deadline are all things a human has to undo or a process has to die of. Errors carry a stable numeric code plus structured data, so a caller matches on the code rather than on a message.
Why ready and heartbeat are requests rather than notifications

A notification cannot report failure, and both of these have a failure to report. For `coord.ready` it is an instance whose entry expired while it was resolving: dropping that silently would leave a service serving, believing it is ready, and invisible to the coordinator forever, with everything consuming it hanging.

`coord.heartbeat` is a request for the same reason one step later. It was a notification at first, on the argument that nothing is lost if one goes missing since the next is a second away. That argument is about a dropped heartbeat and it holds. The failure it misses is a heartbeat that arrives and finds no entry to refresh — a coordinator that expired an instance which had already readied, through a stalled process, a paused virtual machine, or a time-to-live set too tight. It cannot say so, and the host goes on heartbeating into a registry that has forgotten it. `coord.ready` is sent once, at startup, so it cannot catch a loss that happens later; the heartbeat is the only call still being made. The cost is one response per host per second, which is nothing.
Op naming

These are application-level op names. The `$peerline/` prefix is reserved for protocol ops and is deliberately not used here, so a coordinator is an ordinary peerline service that happens to answer these.
What a service declares about itself, and the coordinates it is given back.

Shared rather than restated because the same values travel on three paths that this contract is only one of: a binary writes `Produced` and `Consumed` into the probe file a supervisor reads without any coordinator involved, and a dashboard renders `Endpoints` and `Binding` without calling an op at all. A second definition here would be a second thing to keep in step, with nothing asserting the two were ever the same shape.

types.name: ServiceEntry
description: One mounted service: its name, where it is reachable, and the contracts it declares.

Endpoints are per mounted service, not per contract. A service's coordinates are a property of where it is mounted, not of what it promises, so a process producing two contracts from one mount reports one entry carrying both — and a binding copies the producing service's endpoints into the reply.

Consumed contracts are carried per service because that is where they are declared, but a coordinator only ever uses the union across an instance's services. Readiness is per host: one process, one registration, one lifecycle, and the process is what a supervisor restarts.

fields.name: service
description: The service's stable name, as it appears in logs. Not an identity — use the instance id for that. One binary may legitimately be run twice under two different names.

fields.name: endpoints
description: How to reach this service, on every transport that actually bound. A service whose every transport failed to bind reports an empty set rather than being left out.

fields.name: produces
description: The contracts this service implements.

fields.name: consumes
description: The contracts this service depends on.

types.name: RegisterArgs
description: Everything one process declares about itself in a single call.

The instance id is supplied by the service, not minted by the coordinator. It is stable — derived from the service name plus its mount coordinates — and identical across restarts of either side, so one service shows one identity in logs, in a dashboard and in a CLI over time; a future pinning policy has a name to pin to; and a collision means two processes are claiming one identity, which is a misconfiguration worth rejecting here rather than discovering later.
It is a plain string rather than a distinct type, matching the instance id on a binding, which is the same value seen from the other side.

fields.name: instance
description: This instance's stable, service-chosen identity.

fields.name: pid
description: The process id, for operators reading a dashboard. Send `0` when unknown, which is also what an absent key means. Nothing dispatches on it, and a platform whose process ids do not fit an unsigned 32-bit integer should send `0` rather than truncate.

fields.name: services
description: Every service this process mounts. An empty list registers a process that declares nothing, which is legal and is how a pure consumer with no mounts announces itself.

types.name: RegisterAck
description: The accepted id, echoed back.
It echoes rather than assigns: a caller that sees its own id come back has confirmation that the coordinator holds the identity it thinks it does.

fields.name: id
description: The registered instance id. Always equal to the `instance` that was sent.

types.name: AwaitReadyArgs
description: Who is waiting, and for how long.

What is waited for is deliberately not re-declared here. Registration already established this instance's consumed contracts, and repeating them would put two sources of truth for one fact on adjacent calls. The args carry only what identifies the wait.

fields.name: instance
description: The waiting instance, as registered.

fields.name: timeout_ms
description: How long to wait before failing with the `unresolved` error, in milliseconds.
There is no "wait forever". A cluster's characteristic failure is silence, and a deadline is what converts silence into a diagnosis.

types.name: Unresolved
description: The data carried on an `unresolved` error: what did not resolve, and — if the contract graph suggests one — the cycle that may be why.

fields.name: instance
description: The instance that gave up waiting.

fields.name: waited_ms
description: How long it waited, in milliseconds, echoing the timeout it was given.

fields.name: unresolved
description: The required contracts that had no ready producer at the deadline. Optional contracts never appear here: they do not gate readiness.

fields.name: cycle
description: A cycle in the registered contract graph that passes through one of the unresolved contracts, as a path with the head repeated at the end, so that it renders directly: `storage/1 -> index/1 -> storage/1`. Empty when no cycle touches the outstanding contracts.

Advisory, and an over-approximation. Collapsing instances into contracts invents cycles that no actual deployment has: with two interchangeable producers of one contract, one of which consumes a second contract produced by a consumer of the first, the contract graph has a cycle while every instance still resolves. So this is a hint printed in an error, never a reason to reject anything.

types.name: ReadyArgs
description: Which instance is now serving.

fields.name: instance
description: The instance, as registered.

types.name: ReadyResult
description: The answer to a ready call.

The unknown-instance arm is a value rather than an error because it names a recoverable state with one defined next step — re-register, then send ready again — and a caller should not have to match an error code to drive its own state machine.
Neither arm carries any key beyond the discriminator, so both are the single-key objects `{"status": "ok"}` and `{"status": "unknown_instance"}`.

variants.name: ok
description: The instance is registered and is now marked ready.

variants.name: unknown_instance
description: No such instance: it never registered, or its entry expired while it was resolving.
Re-register and send ready again. Do not re-run the await-ready stream, which is a one-shot startup step whose bindings the caller already holds.

types.name: Heartbeat
description: Which instance is still alive.

fields.name: instance
description: The instance, as registered.

types.name: HeartbeatResult
description: The answer to a heartbeat.

Its own shape rather than a reuse of the ready result, because the two answer different questions — "you are now marked serving" and "you are still known here" — and a shared type would make a future arm on one an unannounced arm on the other. The wire form is identical today, which is what lets a caller handle both with the same branch.

variants.name: ok
description: The instance is registered; its last-seen time has been refreshed.

variants.name: unknown_instance
description: No such instance: its entry expired, or the coordinator restarted since it registered.
Re-register, and send ready again if already serving. Do not re-run the await-ready stream.

types.name: ServiceEndpoints
description: One service's current coordinates, as an update reports them.
Why this is not a service entry

A service entry carries produced and consumed contracts as well as endpoints, and both of those default to empty. An update built out of one could not say "my coordinates changed" without also appearing to say something about the contracts it declares — and since the empty list is both the default and a meaningful value, a coordinator could not tell an update that omitted them from one that withdrew them. The declarations belong to registration and to nothing else, so the shape that carries an update has no field for them.

fields.name: service
description: Which mounted service these coordinates belong to, spelled exactly as the registration spelled it. A name the registration did not declare is not an error and is ignored: it names nothing the coordinator holds.

fields.name: endpoints
description: Where that service is reachable now, on every transport that is still answering.

Empty is legal and meaningful: it says this service can no longer be dialled on anything. That is the same state a service whose every transport failed to bind is registered in, and it makes the service unselectable rather than removing it.

types.name: UpdateArgs
description: Where this instance is reachable now, in full.
This is the whole set, not the part that changed. The coordinator replaces what it holds, so a registered service absent from the list is left with no coordinates at all.

What it deliberately does not carry: the process id, the produced and consumed contracts, or anything else registration established. An update is not a re-registration. It does not clear readiness, it cannot collide on an instance id, and it cannot be refused for cardinality, because it changes nothing any of those three are about. A process that has really changed what it declares has restarted, and a restart re-registers.

fields.name: instance
description: The instance whose coordinates these are, as registered.

fields.name: services
description: Every service this process mounts, with the coordinates it is serving on right now.

An empty list is legal and says the whole instance is unreachable: every transport it had is gone, and it is still running. It is not a deregistration — the entry stays, its consumed contracts still gate its own readiness, and the time-to-live is still what eventually removes it.

types.name: UpdateAck
description: The instance whose coordinates were replaced, echoed back.

It echoes for the reason a registration acknowledgement does: a caller that sees its own id come back has confirmation that the coordinator applied the replacement to the entry it meant. Its own shape rather than a reuse of the registration acknowledgement, because the two answer different questions and a field added to one would otherwise be an unannounced field on the other.

fields.name: id
description: The instance id that was updated. Always equal to the `instance` that was sent.

types.name: ResolveArgs
description: Which contract to resolve, and who is asking.

fields.name: contract
description: The contract to resolve.

fields.name: instance
description: Who is asking, if the caller is a registered instance.

Absent because resolve is also how an operator's CLI asks who could serve a contract, and that caller has no identity to give. When it is present, the coordinator records the producer it handed back as this instance's current selection, which is what makes the bindings op track a consumer that re-resolved after a dropped connection rather than reporting the producer it was first given.
Omit the key entirely rather than sending `null`.

types.name: ResolveResult
description: Every ready producer of the contract, best first.

Ordered by the coordinator's selection policy: the first entry is the coordinator's choice and the rest are alternates, in preference order. A consumer re-resolving after a dropped connection normally takes the first and only looks further if it cannot dial it.
An empty list means no ready producer, which is not an error: a producer may simply not have finished starting.

fields.name: bindings
description: Ready producers, best first.

types.name: SingletonOccupied
description: The data carried on a `singleton_occupied` error.

It names both ends, because neither is in the caller's hand: the refused process knows what it declared but not who already holds the contract, and the operator reading the message needs the incumbent's instance id to go and stop it.

fields.name: contract
description: The contract that admits only one live producer.

fields.name: instance
description: The instance that was refused — the one that just registered.

fields.name: holder
description: The instance already producing the contract. Still live: it heartbeated within the time-to-live, or it would have been swept before the check ran.

fields.name: disagreed
description: Whether the two producers disagreed about the cardinality — one of them declared `single` and the other `any`.

The refusal is the same either way, since the strict reading wins, but the diagnosis is not. With both declaring `single`, somebody started two of a service that admits one. With a disagreement, the two binaries hold different beliefs about the contract and one of them needs fixing whatever else is done about the duplicate.

types.name: InstanceInfo
description: One registered instance, as a listing or a watch reports it.

fields.name: instance
description: Its stable, service-chosen id.

fields.name: pid
description: Its process id, or `0` if it did not report one. Always written, unlike on registration, where an absent key is read as `0`.

fields.name: ready
description: Whether it has sent ready. Only ready instances are ever handed out.

fields.name: last_seen_ms
description: Milliseconds since its last heartbeat, or since registration if it has not heartbeated yet.
Meaningless without the time-to-live to compare it against, which is why a listing carries that too.

fields.name: services
description: Everything it mounts.

fields.name: waiting_on
description: The required contracts it is parked on right now, if it is inside an await-ready call. Empty for an instance that is not waiting.
This is the field that answers the question a stuck cluster actually poses — who is waiting for what — without correlating log files.

fields.name: unreachable
description: The names of this instance's services that reported no coordinates on any transport, and so cannot be dialled by anybody.

A service whose every transport failed to bind is still registered: dropping it would silently drop its consumed contracts from the host's readiness union, which is worse than an unreachable service. But it is then a service that is running, may be ready, and can never be selected — and until this field existed that fact appeared only in the producer's own log, so an operator watching a consumer fail to resolve had nothing in the registry to point at.

types.name: Listing
description: The whole registry as the coordinator currently holds it, with expired instances already swept, and the coordinator itself.
Why the coordinator describes itself here
Two facts about the coordinator are needed to read its own answer, and nothing else in the reply carries them.

The last-seen figure on each instance is meaningless without the time-to-live to compare it against: 9.4 seconds since the last heartbeat is perfectly healthy at a two-minute time-to-live and within a rounding error of fatal at ten seconds. A reader that does not know which cannot colour a row, and an operator that does not know cannot decide whether to worry.

And the address is the only thing that says which coordinator answered. A coordinator deliberately does not register with itself, so an operator with two of them running — a stale one on the default socket, the real one somewhere else — otherwise has no way to tell from the output which they are looking at.

fields.name: ttl_ms
description: How long an instance survives without a heartbeat, in milliseconds. `0` from a coordinator too old to report it, which is also what an absent key means.

fields.name: address
description: Where this coordinator is listening, as an operator would type it — normally a Unix socket path, though nothing here requires it to be one.
Empty when it was not told its own address, which is a coordinator embedded in another process rather than a misconfiguration.

fields.name: instances
description: Every live instance, ordered by instance id — the same order selection uses, so a reader sees the registry the way the coordinator does.

types.name: WatchEvent
description: One frame of the watch stream.
Why there are only three arms

A watch is a snapshot followed by deltas, and the registry is a map keyed by instance id — so structurally there are exactly three things a frame can say: here is everything, here is one entry's current state, this entry is gone. A consumer that applies them to a map by id ends up with the same listing the coordinator holds, which is precisely what the two-second poll this op replaces used to fetch whole.

The causes an observer might care about — registered, became ready, endpoints changed, started or stopped waiting — are deliberately not arms. They are all "this instance's state changed", they all carry the same payload, and a consumer that wants to distinguish them can: it is holding the previous state for that id, so not-was-ready and is-ready is "became ready" and needs no help from the wire. Spending an arm per cause would fix today's list of interesting transitions into the protocol, and every later one would be a breaking change to an internally tagged union. Three structural arms close the set instead.

Removal carries no reason for the same reason it needs none today: the registry has exactly one way to lose an instance, the time-to-live sweep. If a deliberate deregistration is ever added it arrives as an additional defaulted field on the remove arm, not as a fourth arm.
Ordering guarantees

The snapshot is always the first frame and arrives exactly once. No change can slip between the snapshot and the first delta: the coordinator takes the snapshot and installs the watcher under a single lock acquisition. Deltas then arrive in the order the registry applied them.

A consumer may receive an upsert for an instance already in its map — that is the normal case, and it means the entry changed — and must treat it as a replace rather than an insert. It may not receive a remove for an id it has never seen.

variants.name: snapshot
description: The registry as it stood the moment this watch was installed. Always the first frame of the stream, and sent exactly once.

fields.name: registry
description: The whole registry: the identical value the list op would have returned at that instant, carrying the coordinator's own time-to-live and address as well as its instances.

Reusing the listing shape rather than restating its fields is the point. The snapshot and the poll it replaces cannot drift into describing the registry differently, and a consumer switching from one to the other reuses its rendering unchanged.

variants.name: upsert
description: One instance's current state, in full. Sent when it registers, when it becomes ready, when it heartbeats, when its endpoints or services change, and when what it is waiting on changes.
Always the complete instance record, never a patch: a partial update would need the consumer to hold a merge rule that the coordinator also holds, and the two would eventually disagree.

fields.name: instance
description: The instance, exactly as the list op would report it now.

variants.name: remove
description: An instance has left the registry: its time-to-live elapsed with no heartbeat.

This is the event polling could not deliver promptly, and the reason a coordinator runs a sweep timer while anyone is watching. Expiry is generated by the sweep, the sweep is lazy, and on a fleet that has gone entirely silent there are no ops left to trigger one.

fields.name: instance
description: The instance id that is gone. Drop it from your view.

types.name: Edge
description: One recorded selection: this consumer was given that producer for a contract.

fields.name: consumer
description: The instance that asked, as registered.

fields.name: contract
description: What it asked for.

fields.name: producer
description: The instance it was given.

fields.name: age_ms
description: How long ago the selection was made, in milliseconds.
A large age is not staleness by itself — a binding that has worked for a week is the normal case — but it does bound how recently the coordinator was in a position to know.

types.name: BindingGraph
description: Every selection the coordinator has made and still believes in.
What a recorded selection is, and is not

It is the coordinator's best knowledge, not a guarantee. The coordinator records the producer it handed to a consumer at the moment it handed it over, through the await-ready stream at startup or through a resolve on a re-resolve. What the consumer did with it is not observable from here: the data path never touches the coordinator, so a consumer that failed to dial the producer and fell back to an alternate in the same resolve result, or that is mid-reconnect right now, has an edge here that is one step out of date. The age on each edge is how stale it might be.

It is still strictly better than the declared contracts a listing returns. With two ready producers of `storage/1`, declarations say only that `fs` consumes it and order `fs` before both; a recorded selection names the one `fs` was given. A superset ordering is safe but coarse, and under redundancy — the thing the selection policy exists to support — it gets coarser exactly as the cluster gets more interesting.
An edge is dropped when either end leaves the registry: a selection pointing at an expired producer describes nothing.

fields.name: edges
description: Every recorded selection, ordered by consumer and then contract — the same stable ordering a listing uses, and for the same reason.

errors.name: instance_exists
description: Registration was given an instance id that is already registered to a different set of services.
Two live processes claiming one identity is a misconfiguration, and retrying cannot fix it, so it is an error rather than a value. It carries no data: the id is already in the caller's hand.
What is not a collision

Re-registering the same id with the same services, declaring the same contracts, is the reconnect path and it succeeds. A service that reconnects, or one restarted while its previous entry is still inside the time-to-live, has to be able to say who it is again without being crash-looped until the entry expires.

Endpoints are not part of the comparison, and neither is the process id. Both change on an ordinary restart — an ephemeral WebSocket port resolves differently every boot and an iroh ticket is minted at bind — while the instance id, derived from the configured coordinates, does not. Comparing them made every restart of such a host a fatal collision for one whole time-to-live. What remains is what the id is a name for: which services this process mounts and what they declare.

A re-registration clears readiness, because it asserts where the service can be reached rather than that it is serving, so a service that is already serving follows it with a ready call. That is also what makes accepting changed endpoints safe: the new coordinates are handed to nobody until the process that reported them says it is serving.

errors.name: unknown_instance
description: The named instance is not registered: the caller never registered, or its entry has already expired.
Raised by the await-ready stream and by the update op. Both name an instance the coordinator is expected to already hold, and neither has anything it can do with an entry that is not there.

The ready and heartbeat ops deliberately do not use this code. They answer a value instead, because those two are lifecycle transitions whose answer a caller branches its own state machine on — each was very nearly a notification, and the argument for making them requests was precisely that the state they report must not be droppable. An update is a plain write against an entry that is supposed to already exist, and "there is no such entry" is what this code already means.
The recovery is identical wherever it comes from: re-register, and send ready again if already serving. Do not re-run the await-ready stream.

errors.name: unresolved
description: The await-ready stream hit its deadline with required contracts still outstanding.

Fatal for the waiting process: it has dependencies it cannot reach and no way to make progress by waiting longer. The data names what was outstanding and, when the contract graph suggests one, a cycle that may be why.

errors.name: singleton_occupied
description: Registration declared a producer of a contract that already has a live producer, and one of the two declared that contract to admit a single producer.
Why this is not the instance-exists error

They are different mistakes with different fixes, and the operator needs to be told which one they made. Instance-exists says two processes are claiming one identity: the ids collide and the deployments differ. This says the ids are perfectly distinct and the contract is the thing that admits only one holder — a second `storage/1` over its own database file is a config with one entry too many, or a stray process started by hand, and the answer is to stop one of them rather than to rename it. Sharing a code would put both under one message that is wrong for one of them.
Why an error rather than a value

A recoverable state with a defined next step is a value, and anything not fixable by retrying is an error. A second producer of a singleton contract is not fixable by retrying. It is fixed by a human removing one of the two, and until then the process that was refused must not go on believing it is part of the fleet — so a host treats this as fatal and exits, which is the loud failure the distinction exists to convert a silent one into.
What is not occupied

The same instance re-registering. A service that reconnects, or that is restarted while its previous entry is still inside the time-to-live, re-registers its own id and must refresh rather than be refused as its own rival. And an incumbent whose registration has expired no longer holds anything: a coordinator sweeps before it checks, so a dead singleton never blocks its own replacement.

ops.name: coord.register
description: Declare an instance's produced and consumed contracts and its dial coordinates. The first call a joiner makes, and the call it repeats whenever it is told its instance is unknown.
Registering does not make an instance ready, and re-registering clears readiness. A service that is already serving follows a re-registration with a ready call.

ops.name: coord.await_ready
description: Wait for this instance's consumed contracts to resolve, receiving one binding per contract as it does.

A one-shot startup step. The stream ends cleanly once every required contract has been bound; optional contracts that never resolve simply yield no binding and do not hold it open. On the deadline it ends with the `unresolved` error instead.

The stream is seeded from current state, so a contract that was already resolvable when the call was made yields its binding immediately rather than waiting for the next change. A joiner must not re-run this op after a later `unknown_instance`: its bindings are already in hand, and re-running it parks the process on dependencies it has already resolved.

ops.name: coord.ready
description: Mark a registered instance as serving.
Sent once, after the await-ready stream has ended cleanly and the process is actually able to answer ops. Only ready producers are ever handed out to a consumer.

ops.name: coord.heartbeat
description: Refresh an instance's last-seen time.

Send it on a repeating interval well under the coordinator's time-to-live, which a listing reports. It is the only call a healthy joiner keeps making, and therefore the only one that can discover that the registry has forgotten it.

ops.name: coord.update
description: Replace where this instance is reachable, without re-declaring what it produces.

Sent mid-serve, whenever the set of transports the sender is actually answering on changes. A process that keeps serving after one of its transports stops listening has coordinates in the registry that name an address which can only fail to dial, and this is how it withdraws them.

It replaces rather than patches, and it covers the whole instance: a registered service the args do not mention is left with no coordinates. See the contract description for why a full set is the only shape that is safe to send twice.
An update is also proof that the sender is alive, so it refreshes the last-seen time exactly as a heartbeat does. A sender that has just sent one need not immediately send the other.

Readiness is untouched. Unlike a re-registration — which asserts where a process can be reached and therefore clears readiness until the process says it is serving again — an update comes from a process that is already serving and says nothing about whether it is. Clearing readiness here would take a host that lost one transport out of every consumer's reach entirely, which is the opposite of the correction being made.
On `unknown_instance`: re-register, and send ready again if already serving. The re-registration carries the current coordinates, so it is itself the update, and nothing further need be sent.

ops.name: coord.resolve
description: The ready producers of one contract, best first.

Two callers use it. A registered consumer re-resolving after a dropped connection sends its own instance id, and the coordinator records the answer as that consumer's current selection. An operator's CLI asking who could serve a contract omits the id and no selection is recorded.
An empty answer is not an error.

ops.name: coord.list
description: Every registered instance and its state, plus the coordinator's own time-to-live and address. What a dashboard or a CLI reads.
Takes no arguments. Any params object sent is ignored, so a caller may send none at all.
An observer that wants to keep a view current should use the watch op rather than calling this on a timer.

ops.name: coord.bindings
description: The producer this coordinator handed to each consumer, per contract.

Takes no arguments. The list op answers what every instance declares; this answers what was actually chosen. The two are different questions, and only the second can order a shutdown under redundancy.

ops.name: coord.watch
description: Watch the registry: one snapshot frame carrying the whole registry, then one frame per change, until the caller cancels.

Takes no arguments. This is what an observer should use instead of polling the list op on a timer, which is simultaneously too slow — a registration is visible up to one poll interval after it happened — and too fast, since every observer pulls the entire registry on every tick whether or not anything changed.
Why a stream and not a publish-subscribe topic

A watch is per consumer and correlated to the request that opened it: it begins with a snapshot taken for that caller and ends when that caller goes away, which is a stream's shape and not a topic's. The await-ready op is the same shape and is the precedent. A topic's shape is one producer fanning identical events out to subscribers who each missed whatever preceded them, and a snapshot would have to be bolted on beside it.

There is a second, decisive reason in this system: the dashboard reaches this op through a TypeScript client that has streaming but no publish-subscribe runtime, so a topic-based watch would work from Rust and have to be hand-rolled in the browser — exactly the demultiplexing a runtime exists to stop applications writing.
Cancellation
Dropping the receiving end cancels the stream and the coordinator forgets the watcher, which is the same cancel-on-drop every other stream op has.
